video.title: The Real Reason We Should Revive Extinct Animals

protocol.status: v2 labeler B (rubric v2), independent of A
protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Lemonfox transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Explanation: 'imagine you're a mad scientist and you want to bring back an extinct animal' -- path one, backbreed a close living relative (how wolves became dogs), and it worked for the quagga, a zebra hunted to extinction by 1883 and brought back in a version. Lands at 123.5; the 'but it's slow' caveat after it is a second point.

Story: Jurassic Park cloned from mosquito DNA, but real cloning needs a whole living cell; biologists froze tissue from the last bucardo, and in 2003 a baby bucardo was born -- 'unfortunately, the first clone had a malformed lung and didn't survive'. Lands on that twist. Needs the Jurassic Park open: the bucardo lines start 'People tried this', which points back. 82s, slightly over.

Take: people online pointed out these aren't really dire wolves, just genetically modified gray wolves -- 'that was intentional'; the project's scientist (inferred from text) wants the fewest edits for healthy animals; they aren't de-extincting the exact animal, 'they're trying to de-extinct what the animal did' (410.0). The 'good headline but not technically accurate' line to 419.2 is acceptable. Starts after 'In fact,'.

Surprising fact and fix: 'every living black-footed ferret alive today are first cousins. Yikes.' -- a genetic bottleneck leaves them vulnerable, so scientists take DNA from a hundred-year-old museum specimen and edit it into living ferrets. Lands at 601.3.

Story: the northern quoll will be extinct in the wild within ten years because it eats toxic invasive cane toads, but a single letter of genetic code makes it resistant; introducing that one change could save the species (650.1). Opens 'Another great example of using minimal gene editing to save a species', which also sets up the payoff; opening at 'the northern quoll' (610.7) is acceptable.

Question and answer: 'Why are we trying to de-extinct animals at all?' Killing the Tasmanian tiger, the island's only apex predator, set off wallaby and kangaroo explosions and let a contagious face cancer spread among Tasmanian devils -- 'a butterfly effect rippling through the food chain', so some say the only way to rebalance is to put the tiger back (721.2).

Surprising finding: 'what happens when you drop a predator back into an environment that hasn't seen it in decades?' A researcher (inferred) put replica thylacines in the bush: after 100+ years the animals still remember it -- foxes and goats they ignore, 'but if they see the thylacine, they are out of it'.

Debate: would a revived thylacine know how to be a predator? A skeptic doubts it'll ever be wild; advocates say the behavior is hardwired -- house cats fed biscuits for hundreds of generations still pounce the moment a mouse runs by (846.3). Speakers inferred from text.

also_ok.why: Five mass extinctions, a sixth now caused by us, 'this sucks for us' -- and the optimistic turn: the tools for bringing animals back can keep them from going extinct. Opens cleanly, but 'the tools we've been talking about' lean on earlier.

Closing take: the real huge-if-true part isn't bringing back animals but keeping today's healthy; 'de-extinction science is conservation science'; 'the real debate isn't what's a dire wolf, it's what responsibility we have to the world we created'. Its support came earlier.

negatives.why: Cold open over 1933 footage ('look at this', 'you see this dog-looking animal') and a teaser that holds back its point.
News-clip montage: 'De-extinction. We can do this. It's no longer science fiction.'
DNA-as-blocks graphic: 'this one tells me the shape of the skull, this one ear size' -- narration of the screen.
Phone-case sponsor read with an ocean-cleanup pitch.
'99.9 percent identical ... wait, 0.1 percent? That's actually a lot' -- tempting, but opens on 'this is the closest living animal' (screen) and is a step in the recipe.
